newsitem.title: nigeria: FOCUS-Nigerian economic plan - vision or mirage?
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Nigerian economic plan - vision or mirage?

text.p: Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha on Tuesday appointed economic liberal Ernest Shonekan to head a committee of experts to plan for growth into the next century.
But analysts are asking whether the government will act on what the committee proposes.
"At the moment the head of state is definitely on board," said one Lagos-based analyst who preferred not to be named.
"Of course there isn't a lot of time considering the size of the task and the need to involve everybody from every sector of society, the military included."

The optimistic view was reinforced on Tuesday when Nigeria took another step towards liberalisation by lifting a ceiling on interest rates -- a key sticking point blocking agreements with the World Bank. That ceiling had made lending unprofitable for banks and restricted the flow investment funds into the economy.
Abacha's "Vision 2010" is to be set out by a non-political committee of intellectuals.

"This is a period of stock taking, a period to get the correct bearing for our nation, a period during which all hands should be on deck," Abacha said in his speech on the 36th anniversary of Nigeria's independence from Britain.
"The prospects for success are brighter now than ever."
The committee will sit for between nine and 12 months, targeting gross domestic product, inflation, agriculture, industrialisation, literacy, health and employment.
"Vision 2010 must be natural not stage-managed; pervasive and based on a consensus .. otherwise its chances are nil," wrote Dele Sobowale in the Vanguard newspaper recently.
Results will first be applied in the 1998 budget year.
"I really don't see why they have to take so long developing another plan. People have been saying for a long time what needs to be done and we are still waiting," one banker said.

Shonekan, a former chairman of conglomerat UAC Nigeria, was appointed interim head of state following the annulment of presidential elections by a previous military government in 1993. After only a few months he was toppled by Abacha.
The annulment of the elections, followed by a rash of strikes and protests and a surge in inflation drove sub-Saharan Africa's largest economy into a recession from which it has yet to recover.

"Shonekan is very much committed to the kind of reforms wanted by the Bretton Woods institutions, but at the same time he is not hardened against the needs of the average Nigerian," one of his associates said.
Vision 2010 is modelled on plans in other countries, notably Malaysia, whose performance Nigeria wants to emulate.

Despite optimistic plans in the past Nigeria has sunk further into poverty as crude oil revenues have shrunk and successive governments changed economic policy priorities and borrowed heavily to pay for them.
Abacha's tight fiscal policy, adopted in 1995, is credited with bringing down annual inflation to around 30 percent from above 80 percent, but there are few signs of growth.
In Washington finance minister Anthony Ani announced the abolition of the interest rate ceiling of 21 percent with immediate effect.
The Nigerian private sector, as well as the World Bank, is pushing for further liberalisation, including revitalisation of the stalled privatisation programme.
"It is time we saw something more than words now, or by the time the right decisions are taken the rest of the world will have got a step further ahead."
